bib.title: FLASK: Fine-grained Language Model Evaluation based on Alignment Skill Sets

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "FLASK: Fine-grained Language Model Evaluation based on Alignment Skill Sets", Seonghyeon Ye*, Doyoung Kim*, Sungdong Kim, Hyeonbin Hwang, Seungone Kim, Yongrae Jo, James Thorne, Juho Kim, Minjoon Seo. Venue as printed: "Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2024" (arXiv:2307.10928v4, 14 Apr 2024). Affiliation as printed: "KAIST" (one line for all authors).

COVERAGE: 54 of 54 pages extracted (157,012 chars). Read in full: pp. 1-9 (main text) and pp. 20-54 (appendices A-K, including all 12 rubrics, 3 grader prompts, 3 difficulty prompts, both source tables). Skimmed only: pp. 10-19 (references; searched for the origin entries). Radar-chart figures give axis labels only, so per-skill human scores in Fig. 2 are not readable.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Skill-specific rubrics correlate better with humans than one overall score, for all three graders.
  number: GPT-4 grader: Spearman 0.680 vs 0.641, Kendall 0.541 vs 0.495, Pearson 0.732 vs 0.673. GPT-3.5: 0.424 vs 0.360 (Pearson flat, 0.449 vs 0.450). Claude: 0.432 vs 0.352. ROUGE-L 0.333.
  setup: 200 randomly sampled instances, 4 models (GPT-3.5, Bard, Vicuna-13B, Alpaca-13B), 10 KAIST labelers, 3 per instance; grader gpt-4-0613. The skill-agnostic baseline is reference-guided (Zheng et al. 2023 prompt) with its single score copied to every skill.
  quote: "Skill-agnostic (GPT-4) 0.641 0.495 0.673 / FLASK (GPT-4) 0.680 0.541 0.732" (Table 1, p. 6)
- claim: Removing the reference answer hurts most; rationale and rubric matter less.
  number: Spearman 0.516 (no reference), 0.634 (no rationale), 0.646 (no rubric) vs 0.680.
  setup: same, GPT-4 grader.
  quote: "– Reference Answer 0.516 0.429 0.566" (Table 1, p. 6)
- claim: Human agreement is moderate; the model agrees with itself far more.
  number: Krippendorff's alpha 0.488 human-human, 0.835 GPT-4 over 3 runs at temperature 1.0; human-model Pearson 0.732. Readability lowest (H-H 0.089), Correctness highest (0.730).
  quote: "Overall 0.488 0.835 0.732" (Table 2, p. 21)
- claim: The 12 skills in 4 abilities.
  number: Logical Thinking (Logical Correctness, Logical Robustness, Logical Efficiency); Background Knowledge (Factuality, Commonsense Understanding); Problem Handling (Comprehension, Insightfulness, Completeness, Metacognition); User Alignment (Conciseness, Readability, Harmlessness).
  where: p. 2; definitions Table 11, p. 38; each has a hand-written 1-5 rubric (Figs. 37-48, pp. 47-50).
- claim: Dataset size and sources.
  number: 1,740 instances from 122 datasets; at most 20 per single-task dataset; inputs over 2048 removed. Largest: Self-Instruct 252, WizardLM 216, Koala 176, Vicuna 80, MMLU 57.
  quote: "resulting in a total of 1,740 instances sourced from 122 datasets" (p. 4; Table 12, pp. 43-45)
- claim: GPT-4 assigns the labels (top-3 skills, one of 10 domains, difficulty 1-5), validated by humans on 200 instances.
  number: 95.22% skill acceptance, 81.32% domain acceptance, difficulty Pearson 0.774 (Spearman 0.779); human difficulty alpha 0.540.
  quote: "We have observed a 95.22% acceptance rate for skill annotation, an 81.32% acceptance rate for domain annotation, and a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.774 for difficulty annotation." (p. 4; App. G.2, p. 34)
  detail: top-3 was chosen because uncapped labelling put Readability/Comprehension on nearly everything; skill order is shuffled per instance because of position bias (App. E, p. 30-31).
- claim: FLASK-Hard uses instance-specific checklists: GPT-4 writes at most 5 subquestions per instance, authors remove duplicates/irrelevant ones, each scored 1-5.
  number: 89 instances, 25 source datasets.
  quote: "EVAL LM first generates at most 5 subquestions (checklists)... Then, we manually remove duplicates or subquestions unrelated to the annotated skillset." (p. 5)
- claim: Finer rubrics are more robust to padding.
  number: same score kept on 43.82% (skill-agnostic), 52.99% (skill-specific), 55.78% (instance-specific).
  setup: GPT-3.5 answers on FLASK-Hard rewritten more verbose by GPT-3.5; Completeness and Conciseness excluded.
  quote: "Robustness 43.82 52.99 55.78" (Fig. 3, p. 6)
- claim: Open models trail on logic and knowledge, nearly match on style.
  number: Logical Robustness: Vicuna 2.26, Tulu-65B 2.66, LLaMA2-70B 2.59 vs GPT-3.5 3.94, GPT-4 4.22. Readability: 4.65 vs 4.86.
  setup: whole set, GPT-4 grader; proprietary versions May-June 2023.
  quote: "Logical Robustness 2.26 2.41 2.66 2.59 3.94 3.47 3.59 4.22" (Table 9, p. 36)
- claim: Proprietary models also drop on FLASK-Hard.
  number: GPT-4 Logical Correctness 4.22 to 3.00; "up to 50% performance degradation for some skills" (p. 2). Instance-specific rubrics score lower overall (no table).
  quote: "Logical Correctness 1.22 1.46 1.78 1.78 2.30 1.70 2.22 3.00" (Table 10, p. 36)
- claim: Cost.
  quote: "model-based evaluation is 22 times cheaper and 129 times faster" ($0.06 vs $1.3 per query; ~2 s vs 257.8 s; Table 8, p. 35)
- claim: Three different grader models agree only at alpha 0.471 (Table 4, p. 27). Response length correlates with Completeness (0.737) and Insightfulness (0.763), less with Logical Correctness (0.147) (Table 5, p. 32).

LIMITS
- Conceded (App. A, p. 20): human study covers 200 instances, 4 models, 10 same-university labelers; central-tendency bias and fatigue; grader prefers longer answers and its own style; English, single-turn, zero-shot only; Hard set is 89 instances, "making the effect of outliers unavoidable".
- Not shown: no human validation of the instance-specific checklists ("we have not conducted human evaluations for the instance-specific scoring rubrics"); their only evidence is the verbosity robustness test. No significance tests or intervals on Table 1; the GPT-4 gain is about 0.04 Spearman. GPT-4 is both grader and a graded model (labelled "Oracle"). Missing reference answers were generated by GPT-4. Domain labels are wrong about 1 in 5.
- Dated: 2023 models (Vicuna, Alpaca, Claude 1.0, Bard); the open-vs-proprietary gap is a snapshot.

BUILDS ON: Rogers et al. (2021) QA skill taxonomy (basis of the 12 skills); Sugawara & Aizawa (2016); Zheng et al. (2023) for the skill-agnostic baseline prompt; Liu et al. (2023) and Wei et al. (2022b) for rationale-before-score; Webb (1997; 1999) and the NIH proficiency scale for difficulty; Reid et al. (2022) for domains; Min et al. (2023) and Krishna et al. (2023) for fine-grained evaluation; Dubois et al. (2023) for inter-model agreement.

CODE (prompts, verbatim)
- Skill-specific (Fig. 34, p. 42): "Make sure to give feedback or comments for each category first and then write the score for each category... The scores of each category should be orthogonal"
- Instance-specific (Fig. 35, p. 46): "Score 5: The response fully satisfies the requirements of the subquestion better than the ground truth answer."
- Sample rubric (Fig. 37, p. 47): "Score 4: The model's response is logically sound, but it does not consider some edge cases."

FIGURES: Figure 1, p. 2. Shows the single-score prompt next to the per-skill prompt, and the same skill under a generic rubric ("avoid logical contradictions?") versus an instance checklist ("consider conditions that alters the proton's kinetic energy?"). It is the fastest way to show rubric versus checklist.

- App. J calls the source list "Figure 12"; it is Table 12. Captions for Tables 9-10 mention Alpaca, which is not in those tables. The Fig. 29 caption has left and right swapped.

- Text extraction was clean; small-caps names are split (e.g. "V ICUNA", "T ¨ULU").
